utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. And good afternoon to those who are in attendance in Tokyo. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could I invite you repeat the case. We -- it's -- becomes a tradition that we start with French on the English channel in the morning. Could you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could I inquire whether my words in whatever language could be understood in Tokyo and that you can see me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I'm happy to report that we can see and hear you clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Monkhouse. I'd first like to inform the parties that the decision delivered by the two remaining Judges yesterday remains in force today. That means that it's in the interests of justice to continue to hear the case in the absence of Judge Kinis. Could I further inquire, Mr. Registrar, who are in the room you're in, in Tokyo at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, Mr. Akashi, myself and, pursuant to the Trial Chamber's request for judicial assistance, a representative of the Japanese foreign affairs is also attending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Monkhouse, for that information. Mr. Akashi you would like to remind you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I would like to remind that you are you still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I fully understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Misetic, are you ready to continue your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Misetic -- good morning, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you one follow-up question to your meeting in Knin on the 7th, or your trip to Knin on the 7th that I didn't ask you yesterday. We looked extensively at the code cable that you prepared after that trip to Knin, and I had asked you whether you had been briefed by the UN personnel in Knin as to any evidence of systematic looting by the Croatian Army, and you said you did not recall that. Had you been briefed to that effect by the United Nations personnel in Knin, would that have been something that you would have included in the code cable to Mr. Annan?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all probability, my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Akashi. Now, picking up where we left off yesterday, you had -- we started talking about the system of reporting and then what measures you would take in the situation where the teams in the field, particularly HRAT, UNMO, UNCIVPOL or UNCRO, would report about human rights violations in the field, and if you received that information, what measures might be taken, and you gave us two examples at the end of the day yesterday. One being that it would be reported to New York; and the second possibility is that you might ask for a meeting with Mr. Sarinic to discuss the matter. Is that -- does that accurately reflect what you stated yesterday?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us why, upon receiving such reports from the field, you would ask for a meeting with Mr. Sarinic?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What was the purpose of asking for a meeting with Mr. Sarinic, for example, if you would receive reports from the field about human rights violations? What would you hope to achieve?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is part my responsibility as SRSG to discourage military conflict and, if possible, to prevent it; in addition, protection for UN personnel as well as innocent civilian populations, and, as well, safe-guarding of their human rights. These are all part and parcel of my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Let me start by turning your attention to the document that is tab 15 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that is Exhibit D1534.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, this is a code cable sent from you, again, to Mr. Annan, on the 16th of August, and it discusses the situation in various sectors. If you could turn your attention to paragraph 7 of this document, which is on page 2.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. The paragraph says: "The arson campaign conducted by the Croatians, which has been under way in Sector South since the 8th of August [sic] has accounted for an estimated 200 houses. Almost the entire towns of Kistanje, Djevrska, and Otric have been torched." Now, to the best of your recollection, is that the information you were receiving as to the total number of houses that had been burned in Sector South as of 16 August?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be positive, but I have no need to question the veracity of information in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show you a clip, a video-clip right now. On the same day as this code cable you, in fact, had a meeting with Mr. Sarinic, and I would like to show you that clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There is -- just one moment. One moment. There is 1D1174. And it's report about your meeting with Mr. Sarinic on the 16th of August.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Bunjevac-Filipovic: The future of the UNCRO mandate and the reduction of the number of its troops were the subject of there morning's meeting between the Chief of Staff of the office of the president of the republic, Hrvoje Sarinic and the Special Representative of the UN Secretary-General, Yasushi Akashi. "Reporter: What can be the conclusion of today's meeting between Sarinic and Akashi? According to Sarinic, the result is not final however both sides are on the same, or rather, good path. "Hrvoje Sarinic: These are a series of meetings during which we will discusses the future UNCRO mandate, the reduction of the forces stationed here. I think that we are on a good path of resolving these issues. You know that a part of UNCRO forces is already leaving Croatia and our discussions are proceeding in this respect. "Reporter: The situation in Slavonia, the repeated attacks of the Serb insurgents on Croatian towns, this is a separate subject. "Hrvoje Sarinic: I have naturally stressed again those basic principles that are guiding Croatian policy in that they must control in the east sector which is naturally, the most delicate at this point the border in the east sector and the part much the border towards Bosnia which is controlled on by the Bosnian Serbs. "Yasushi Akashi: The situation is tense with occasional shellings on both sides, but I believe that there isn't any prospect of major fighting taking place. I bring this conclusion on the basis of contacts and dialogues between the head of Osijek and Baranja county and the representative of the former Sector East. "Reporter: The next meeting between Sarinic and Akashi is scheduled to take place in a couple of days."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- it seems that the topics of conversations, at least as reported there, and according to your comments and Mr. Sarinic's comments --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wondered, Mr. Kehoe, whether the transcript was already -- we don't not only have to wait for the translation but also for the transcript. But for the time being, please proceed. But I think that the transcript is yet not complete at this point, the transcript is not complete, but perhaps difficult to ... Yes, it will be completed later. But not only the translation but also the transcript needs our attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise to the court reporter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, in that video-clip --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- it seems that on the 16th of August, according to the news report and the reported comments made by you and Mr. Sarinic, that the topic of conversation seemed to be deployment of UNCRO troops and the situation there Eastern Slavonia. And I'd also like to show you a code cable that you prepared on the 17th, and this is tab 78 in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the video be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Was there a question put to the witness rather than the comment from Mr. Misetic, is -- that being said, we don't object to the admission of it. But I'm just wondering --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is still to follow, Mr. Misetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in view of the fact there are no objections and we will hear questions about it. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D1658.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1658 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Akashi, tab 78 in your binder is 65 ter 2404.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this it? Uh-huh. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is the code cable for the -- it says -- dated 17 August, but if you look at the first paragraph, it begins by talking about yesterday which obviously would be the 16th of yesterday, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I think we have a problem on getting it on our screen and what I saw from your Case Manager, there was some problem with the number which apparently has now been resolved. We are now looking at 65 ter? Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are looking at 65 ter numbers 2404.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Again, the document refers to events that took place on the 16th of August, and if we go to paragraph 2 towards the middle, there's a reference to this meeting that we saw in the video-clip. And it says, Mr. Akashi -- sorry, the topic was: "There are growing indications that forced repatriation of those refugees to Velika Kladusa area may begin today. Mr. Akashi raised this issue with Mr. Sarinic yesterday in a meeting between the two and was given assurances of cooperation by the Croatian authorities and adhering to the international standards for the protection of the refugees." Now, there doesn't appear to be any further reference in the code cable to the meeting with Mr. Sarinic on the 16th. My question to you, based on both the video and the code cable, is: Do you have any reason to believe that you raised any issues of -- concerning human rights reports with Mr. Sarinic on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Obviously my question -- I hope you understood, I meant human rights in Sector South. Obviously the issue of the Bosnian Muslim refugees in Velika Kladusa was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that 65 ter 2404 be marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D1659.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. I'd like to put a follow-up question in this respect. Mr. Akashi, from the fact that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- neither in the video --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- nor in this cable anything is said about human rights or violation of human rights concerns in Sector South. Could we conclude that they were non-existent at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my supposition is that in those circumstances, raising the human rights questions would not have been unnatural or illogical. So I would not attribute too much meaning to the fact that -- the difference to it is missing from one cable or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're going through a series of these just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- so if I could complete the line of question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just for the transcript, I may have misunderstood. I just want to -- if it possible to clarify if someone else understood. Was it "a natural or illogical" or "natural or a logical"? I missed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I repeat, My Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that from simple lack of reference to human rights, we cannot necessarily deduce that there was no discussion of these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you used a few words on which Mr. Hedaraly seeks clarification, especially in view of what we see in front of us as our transcript. Did you say that raising the human rights question would not have been a unnatural or an un-logical matter to raise. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, My Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Akashi, who was Phillip Arnold?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Huh? I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who was Phillip Arnold?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was my press spokesman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Akashi, I have another video which -- this is from the 22nd of August, 1995. This is Mr. Arnold, your press spokesman, in a video-clip, which I believe is 22 minutes on a programme called Slikom na Sliku, which is a national TV programme on the evening news broadcast in Croatia. And in these 22 minutes - I believe I have asked for a stipulation on this so we don't have to play the video - but Mr. Arnold doesn't discuss any issue of human rights violations in the newly liberated territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could ask the Prosecution whether they're willing to stipulate to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think the e-mail correspondence was CC'd to the Chamber. And I think I had expressed the Prosecution's position at that time, which is still the same, which is if we can have the transcript of it, we can review it and see if there is any relevance. The little clip that has been put on the exhibit list for this witness that we have reviewed has a question and answer series, and none of the questions referred to Sector South, so obviously to then conclude from that, that there is no reference to crime just is completely irrelevant. So if we can have the transcript of the full 22 minutes, if that's what Mr. Misetic is seeking a stipulation for, which we had asked now whenever we got the request, then we will be able to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, when was the e-mail copied to the Chamber? Could you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It was early August, Mr. President, and Mr. Hedaraly has had a complete transcript of the entire video along with the entire video. It's 65 ter 1D1173. It's also in the binder at tab 20 and it's the entire 22 minutes were, in fact, transcribed, translated at Mr. Hedaraly's request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now it seems that Mr. Hedaraly is more hesitant to adopt any conclusions from that rather than that he would be un-waiving, unwilling to stipulate that the issue was not mentioned. Where you say, if you don't ask about it, you'll get no answers in relation to that issue. Now, Mr. Hedaraly, let's focus first on conclusions, have you reviewed the full transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I have reviewed the five pages of transcript that was a -- with the 65 ter number that we received. If that is the full 22 minutes, then I can say I have reviewed the complete, if that is those five pages of transcript, then I have -- I thought 22 minutes would be much longer than five pages, so I thought it was the just a small portion that I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not everyone is talking so quickly that it fills pages and pages. Mr. Misetic, are the five pages the full transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The reason the video is long is because the translations going back and forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Stipulation apparently sought by Mr. Misetic is whether the issue violations of human rights and commission of crimes is appearing in this transcript, in this video, Mr. Misetic proposing to you that it cannot be found in it. Could you stipulate on that, apart from what conclusions would you draw from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Sure. But then I guess -- I would wonder what the relevance of that stipulation or of that fact would be if then there would be no conclusion that we felt would be relevant as a result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I think, as a matter of fact, of course, in terms of conclusions that you would say it's irrelevant because you can't draw any conclusions. Mr. Misetic, I take it, will attach some weight to it in drawing conclusions and find the relevance in that, and then the stipulation in itself seems not to be problematic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm -- maybe I'm misunderstanding something, and if I am, I apologise. The stipulation in itself, I don't see how that can assist the Chamber without the Chamber having actually the context in which that interview was made, what questions were posed; so it's not only a matter of what conclusion to draw from it from the Prosecution standpoint, which we question, but also just a stipulation standing like this, that this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that Mr. Misetic proposes to tender the document. That would include all the questions, but in order to save time in Court, not to invite the witness to read through it in full and then to find -- to come to the same -- I should avoid the word "conclusion." But to come to the same finding that no violations of human rights or commission of crimes are mentioned in that interview. That's what, apparently, Mr. Misetic is looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's fine. The original e-mail was a stipulation in lieu of the transcript. If the transcript is in evidence, then there is no problem with that stipulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic that is what you intended to achieve?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we don't have to bother the witness reading five pages to find what every person who can read could find. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, Mr. President I ask that that exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence, 65 ter 1D1173.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D1660.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1660 is admitted into evidence. And the stipulation is on the record, that commission of crimes or violations of human rights were not mentioned during this interview questions and answers. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, if we could then turn to a meeting that took place between you and Mr. Sarinic on the 2nd September. And I'd like to show you an another video-clip of that meeting, which is 65 ter 1D1175.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Reporter: UN Secretary-General Special Representative arrived in Zagreb after talks with the representatives of so-called Serb authorities in Erdut on the temporarily occupied territory of the Republic of Croatia. "Yasushi Akashi: Sector East leadership has accepted UNCRO's proposal for a new mandated which included border monitoring between Croatia and the so-called FRY/Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and which also includes the implementation of the cease-fire agreement from 29 March 1994. "Reporter: On the border between the Republic of Croatia and the so-called FRY in the former Sector East, as Akashi explained, nine check-points will be established and regarding other border areas with the so-called FRY, including Prevlaka and Dubrovnik, UN military observers will remain in those areas. Akashi also commented on the talks with the military commanders in former Sector East who have, as Akashi said, affirmed their willingness to adhere to the cease-fire and find a peaceful resolution. According to Akashi, a meeting is scheduled to take place on Monday between the commander of the Osijek Military District, General Djuro Decak and the Serb General Dusan Loncar. In expressing his gratification over the talks which are topics for negotiations on the peaceful reintegration of Sector East of the constitutional system of Republic of Croatia Hrvoje Sarinic stated. "Hrvoje Sarinic: We are on the way of establishing a kind of temporary administration there which would primarily ensure the return of the displaced persons, and afterwards, naturally, the complete peaceful reintegration of that area that to the constitutional system of the Republic of Croatia. "Reporter: Answering reporters' questions on Croatia's positions regarding the latest American peace initiative, Sarinic stated that Croatia will participate in proposals, which are acceptable to them but also sufficiently realistic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Akashi, do you recall --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you there question: From this video it again doesn't appear that human rights issues in Sector South were a topic of conversation. Do you recall having any meeting with Mr. Sarinic from the -- from the 7th of August until -- and through the 2nd of September, specifically on the issue of human rights violations taking place in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I was not in Croatia throughout this period you referred to. I left Zagreb on the -- on the -- on the 17th of August to return to New York. It was partly to attend the wedding of my daughter, and then I returned to Zagreb on the 23rd of August, as -- and I cannot give you a specific answer whether human rights questions, were raised or not raised in my frequent meetings with Mr. Sarinic in the course of my actual presence in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Akashi --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- from what I see from here, Mr. Akashi, you're consulting what appears to be a diary and you do it with such precision that even a magnifying-glass assists you. That's -- as I said before, if you want to consult anything, well, we can see it so there's no problem. Whenever you want to consult any notes or any documentary materials, you're invited to tell us, but it's now on the record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I ask that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Inadvertently, my age shows up, apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, I would ask that 65 ter 1D1175 be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D1661.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1661 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, I'd like to you take a look at the document which is at tab 18 in your binder. And this is 65 ter 1710.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. This is a code cable drafted by -- or I'm sorry, sent by you to Mr. Annan on the 9th of September, documenting your meeting with Mr. Sarinic on that day. And there a lot of issues that you discussed with him. But if we turn to paragraph 6, which is at page 2, it seems that Mr. Sarinic complained -- let me just read. He says: "He made particular mention of our press and information reports on mass graves as having had an effect on the international community. He insisted that these reports were untrue and should be retracted. He also insisted that the Croatians, particularly General Cermak, had provided UNCRO with all the necessary details to refute such claims. I assured Sarinic that all our reports were factual and refrain from making any sweeping judgements in our press releases. However, while I did not in any way associate the continued burning and looting in Sectors North and South with the government, in some case, Croatian Army and police had been seen in the vicinity of such incidents." And if we go to your witness statement, at paragraph 13, you mention this meeting. You said: "On 9 September 1995, I raised incidents of burning of property with Hrvoje Sarinic. I do not recall raising concerns about the Croatian government being behind the burning, because I did not consider the Croatian government in the narrow, strict sense to be the perpetrator of these acts. I thought that there were individual criminal elements not part of the Croatian government who might have been doing these things, including order criminal, paramilitary groups and roving gangs. Had I received reports that the Croatian government was behind the burning and looting of Serbian property, I certainly would have raised it with Hrvoje Sarinic. This would have been part of my duties as the Special Representative."

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, what is reported in those official cables, from my Zagreb headquarters to New York, should be considered as overriding whatever information I may have discussed -- I told you on the phone several weeks ago, because my present memory is not certainly as detailed or as accurate as the information I was communicating to headquarters in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, Mr. Akashi. But my question to you is: Do you recall ever raising a issue with Mr. Sarinic to the effect that, in fact, the government was behind burning and looting?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just want to refer back to the cable you mentioned several minutes ago, which make some specific references to the acts of Croatian Army and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But other than that paragraph, which, again, says you did not associate the continued burning and looting with the government, my question is: Do you recall at any time raising an issue that the government was behind a campaign of burning and looting?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be specific, but in those circumstances, all kinds of crimes of commission and omission were discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall anything specifically?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, my present memory is not very specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that 65 ter 1710 be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Which one is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The code cable of the 9th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is will be Exhibit D1662.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, I'd ask to you turn to exhibit -- well, let me ... Exhibit 25 -- or, sorry, tab 25 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, this is 65 ter 1D1589.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now this is a memo to you from Mr. Annan, and it's dated 16 October 1995 and says at paragraph 1: "During Security Council consultations today, the Russian delegation made the following requests ..." And then paragraph 1 (b)(1) says that: "According to information received by his delegation," which would be the Russian delegation, "in 320 villages visited by UN personnel, 22.000 houses had been burnt." And I'm going to ask you a question about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. President, if I could have this one marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D1663.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1663 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, if you could turn to the next tab, which is tab 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, this is 65 ter 1D1591.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And this is your response to Mr. Annan, dated the 17th of October. I'm sorry, I failed to read to that you paragraph 1 (b)(5) of that code cable from Mr. Annan to you said: "Could the UN have access to reports by the OSCE coming out the Vienna on the situation in Croatia. One report had said that of 21.000 homes visited in the Krajina, 15.000 had been destroyed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we go back to that so that we could follow your reading, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is D1663. It's the next page, please. It's the paragraph (5) at the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, tab 26 - this is 1D1591 -

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- and you write: "Further to paragraph 1 (b)(5) of your MSC-3268, we believe the statistics mentioned in your cable concerning destruction of property are based on a survey conducted by UN Military Observers, which is refers to in a report by ECMM. To our knowledge, no monitors, other than UNMOs, have visited 21.000 homes in the area." Now, Mr. Akashi, do you recall, first of all, what this UN Military Observer survey was about?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the responsibility of UN Military Observers, or UNMOs, to be brief, to constantly monitor the situation under their responsibility and give us their reports, and so this is part of their standard responsibility, and this is simply one example of many such reports they make.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm asking you now specifically: Do you recall receiving a report from UNMO which would indicate that out of 22.000 houses in Sector South, 16.000 had been destroyed or partially destroyed?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection of that particular report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, would that be something that would have stuck in your memory, that 16.000 out of 22.000 houses had been destroyed, had you received that information?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I cannot tell you one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this exhibit, 65 ter 1D1595 be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are no objections from Mr. Hedaraly. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is will be Exhibit D1664.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1664 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, while we're on this document, do you have any knowledge or any reason to believe that before the -- this memo of the 17th of October, you had sent any information to Mr. Annan indicating that UNMOs were reporting that 16.000 houses had been destroyed or partially destroyed in Sector South up until that time?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to believe that prior to this memo of the 17th of October, 1995, you had informed New York of reports by UNMO that 16.000 houses had been destroyed or partially destroyed in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If such a fact had been reported by UNMOs, it is most probable that I have received such information and I would have transmitted -- transmitted it to New York headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me follow up on that answer. Obviously we can see from the code cables that you dealt with Mr. Annan on a mostly a daily basis. Looking at these two memos - in other words, the memo from Mr. Annan to you asking for an explanation, given what the Russian delegation was claiming in the Security Council and your reply to him - if you, in fact, had already told him of that information, if you had relayed to him previously the findings of UNMO, can you explain why Mr. Annan would have sent you such a memo on the 16th of August, and why in your memo back you wouldn't have just referred back to any earlier correspondence, in which you had previously already advised him of this?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Kofi Annan sent me this cable because of questions were raised on the matter in the Security Council, but I have no background as to whether UNMOs have made previous report, or reports, to us on this matter. I -- I am -- I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, page 22, line 17 start with the 16th of August, although the request by Mr. Annan was dated the 16th of October, and the response was the 17th of October. Did you want to refer to anything else than the 16th of October?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was a mistake. Then we understand your question to relate to the 16th of October request by Mr. Annan to Mr. Akashi in relation to matters raised in the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, let me show you an exhibit which is marked -- I believe it is P97. This is tab 80 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If you look at the heading, it's dated 13 September 1995, and it was sent to UNMO HQ Zagreb. And now this --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- gives some allegations concerning a survey done by the UNMOs, and it says, if you look at numbered paragraph 1, under "Main basic conclusions/findings": "As on 13 September ... out of 18.232 houses in 240 villages ... checked by UNMO, more than 13.600, or 73 per cent, houses have been completely or partly burnt/destroyed after Operation Storm. Approximately 650 houses or only" -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "... or 5 per cent had been destroyed before 4 August." Now looking at this document and comparing it with the memos in October that we just looked at, my question is, first of all, do you recall seeing anything like this in September of 1995?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a positive answer -- to you whether I had seen such a report prior to this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you then a general question first. Based on your knowledge of how your office functioned as the Special Representative for the Secretary-General, if, on the 13th of September, your office had received information that following Operation Storm, 73 -- 73 per cent of houses in Sector South had been completely or partly burnt or destroyed after Operation Storm, would that have been something that you would raise with Mr. Sarinic?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would appear, on the face of it, that this constitutes a serious enough violation and would have been an appropriate matter of my discussion with Mr. Sarinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me see if I can -- if I understand your testimony, however, Mr. Akashi. You have no recollection of having seen such a report, and you have no recollection of ever having raised this issue with Mr. Sarinic?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, you are referring to the situation 14 years ago, and we were involved in a number of critical situations, not just in Croatia but in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I think I should be forgiven for -- if I do not recall all these details of exchanges which have taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, based on your knowledge of how your office functioned, Mr. Akashi, would we expect -- or would you expect that we would find a code cable from you to Mr. Annan passing this information along somewhere on or near the 13th of September, 1995, if, in fact, you had received this information?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I understand your memory has faded, Mr. Akashi, so let me ask you as to how your office functioned. If your office received information that you see in this report, would normal procedure be to relay this information in a code cable to Mr. Annan?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in the normal course of events I -- my office would, in all probability, have transmitted such information to New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if you had had a meeting with Mr. Sarinic on this issue, would you expect or would normal procedure be that you would document that meeting with Mr. Sarinic on this topic in a code cable to Mr. Annan?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say yes. But, as you know, there were so many meetings with Sarinic, each meeting dealing with a number of urgent questions. But in the course of these meetings the kind of events mentioned in this particular cable would have come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Akashi, let me ask you about something which I believe you have some knowledge of. The Secretary-General, you're aware, would, in this time-period, periodically submit reports to the Security Council on the situation in Croatia and throughout the former Yugoslavia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And in his preparation of his reports, would you send him or assist him, I should say, in preparing those reports to the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly I would have -- or, rather, my office would have assisted Secretary-General's office in preparing these reports to the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask to you look at tab 43 of your binder. And this is, Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 1D2932. I'm sorry, I'm told I need to seek leave to add this to our 65 ter exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Is that the 23 August report to the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm getting to that one next, but this is the 29 September report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The further report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, there is a paragraph 5, it's on the first page --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- in this report to the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There's references to continuing reports of human rights abuses and of the looting and burning of houses. And if we go to page 4, paragraph 14.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "The Croatian government has stated that Serbs are welcome to live in Croatia and that those Serbs who fled following the recapture of Sectors West, North and South are welcome to return. However, UNCRO continues to receive from its Human Rights Action Teams well-documented reports of human rights abuses and destruction of property. The incidents described in those reports do nothing to restore confidence among the Serb minority. A continuing United Nations presence in Croatia will provide one means of monitoring human rights ..." and then it goes on.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you wish, can you take a look through this report, but there is no mention in this further report of the Secretary-General, of the statistics in the UNMO report, which you looked at prior to this document of the 13th of September about 73 per cent of homes being totally or partially burnt/destroyed in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now let me ask you this question: If your office had, in fact, received such a report from UNMO, would that statistic have made it into the Secretary-General's further report on the 29th of September?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. I think these reports on the situation in Gracac from the Secretary-General to the Security Council are of rather general information or character, and partly in the interests of conciseness, the -- give the gist of considerations and conclusions which Secretary-General considers necessary and important to give to the Council members. So they are not necessarily exhaustive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So you think -- well, let me ask you this: Do you think this report conveys the gist of an UNMO report that 15 to 16.000 houses had been burnt down in Sector South since the 4th of August and that total, 73 per cent of houses in the sector, is it your position that this further report of the Secretary-General contains that, as you call it, gist?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, for instance, the information contained in paragraph 14 of this report before us gives sufficient information on the seriousness of the situation, and I think explains enough as to why many refugees, at that point in time, had still -- were still hesitant who go back to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, can you complete your answer, Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that 65 ter 1D2932 be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is will be Exhibit D1665.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Misetic, for my understanding of paragraphs 5 and 15, you referred to paragraph 5 as stating continuous violations of human rights. Am I wrong if I read paragraphs 5 and 14 as primarily focussing on return of those who had left and that in paragraph 5 the focus is not primarily on the -- well, to say the -- the -- the numbers of houses, but, rather, on this to continue, which would keep people off from returning as was hoped they would do. I'm just trying to understand the document and whether I'm missing something, if I read 5 and 15 as having its primary focus not on establishing exactly how much damage was there but on what kept people off from returning, in which context violation of human rights and damage done, looting, et cetera, played a role. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I understand that that is the general topic of the report. However, obviously I think you can anticipate that our position is going to be -- what our position is going to be on specifically the statistics in the UNMO report and the direct relevance they would have to an issue of return of Serbs. I mean, if 73 per cent of the homes have been burned down, that might be a factor to consider in whether it's feasible for these people to return in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say that main reason for not returning is that there would be no houses anymore rather than.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand your point. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, if we could -- if I could turn your attention to tab 48.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is it 65 ter 1D1164.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And this is now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, the Secretary-General submitted an earlier report to the Security Council on the 23rd of August, and this is a memo from you to Mr. Annan, in which, it would appear, that you are attaching a draft of that report -- sorry, a revised version of a draft you had submitted on the 20th of August of -- for the Secretary-General to submit to the Security Council. And first my question to you is: Do you recall the report? Generally speaking, do you recall that after Operation Storm, your office was working on preparing a draft report for the Secretary-General to submit to the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us -- this refers to -- obviously the report was prepared pursuant to Security Council Resolution 1009 of the 10th of August. And my first question to you is: In terms of methodology, what process would your office have gone through to gather information for the report? Can you explain what steps were taken, in order to obtain information?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through our extensive presence in various areas of Croatia - particularly in the so-called UN Protected Areas - we have both military and civilian personnel, including UNMOs who monitor the situation and assess the situation from human rights, humanitarian, and security viewpoints. So I think we have in this instances followed standing procedures to gather such information and digest it in such a way that it can be made into a very short, concise and precise report. Usually these drafts are exchanged between Zagreb and New York. They undergo some amendments and only when they are finalised they'll be printed in the form of a Security Council document from the Secretary-General.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So the actual gathering of information would go through -- would be done by UNMO, and you indicated military and civilian personnel. Would that be UNCIVPOL?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot give you a comprehensive list of all those people who might be involved, but, you know, we have, in addition to UNCRO in the case of Croatia, we have UNHCR and other UN-related organisations and -- but we always try to verify the information. We do not blindly accept any information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could -- if you could go to the draft, which is page 3 of this document at numbered paragraph 5. There, in your draft, the first sentence reports: "On 4 August 1995, the Croatian Army launched an attack in Sectors North and South and Knin fell on 5 August following concentrated shelling." I'm going to ask you some questions about that when we look at the next document. But if we could now go to paragraph 18, your draft indicates: "Representatives of the International Committee for the Red Cross have been given favourable reports concerning the access they have been given to all persons detained in connection with the recent conflict by Croatian authorities." The last sentence says: "The majority of those originally detained have been released and many of those who remain in detention have been transferred from collective centres to district prisons." Is that consistent with your recollection of what the ICRC had indicated were the conditions of persons who had been detained in connection with the recent conflict?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I have no specific recollection as to the role ICRC was playing in this particular instance, but in the course of normal events, cooperation between UN and ICRC is such that, in this area of ICRC competence, they would provide us with this kind of information. And in view of their high reputation, I think we made use of this information they gave us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this exhibit be marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D1666.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Akashi, if I could turn your attention to tab 16 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is Exhibit P64.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is an UNMO report concerning a survey of -- or a provisional assessment of damage caused by HV operations from the 4th to the 6th of August. And it talks about how an UNMO team Podkonje made a provisional assessment. And paragraph 2 reported that: "In general, shelling was concentrated against military objectives. The damage is caused by shelling to civilian establishments is concrete to the close vicinity of military objectives. Only few, three to five impacts, is observed in other urban areas." My question, Mr. Akashi, you have now testified that UNMOs and UNCIVPOL would be the information gatherers for you to prepare the draft report for the Secretary-General. Do you recall this report and whether it -- this survey was conducted in anticipation of the report that you were assisting with -- assisting the Secretary-General with --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not think so. Mr. Misetic, these kinds of UNMO reports pour into our Zagreb headquarters on a daily basis, and so it is most unlikely that they were prepared specifically in preparation for, or, in anticipation of the report of the Secretary-General to the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this question: The first sentence in paragraph 2 talks about the shelling was concentrated. And paragraph 5, which is, again, tab 48 of your binder of your draft report which I had shown you earlier, says that Knin fell on 5 August following concentrated shelling. Can you tell us where your information came from in your draft report to the Secretary-General that the shelling in Knin was concentrated?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I cannot tell you where the information came from. It may have come from multiple sources including this particular report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That leads me to my next question, which is tab 17 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which is Exhibit P228.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: UNCIVPOL did its assessment of damage in Knin. And if you look at paragraph 2, it covers -- sorry. It states: "We covered the whole township and observed several impacts of shells/rockets around the Tvik factory, milicija headquarters, general direction of northern barracks (shells coming from north-east) and between the government house (white house), Knin radio and TV building and the hill-side below Knin castle." Now, your previous answer indicated that your information and report could have come from multiple sources concerning the nature of the shelling in Knin. Would this also be such a report that may have been prepared -- sorry, that may have been considered in drafting your report?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is entire possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And let me ask you about this document. Looking at this document, would this assessment have been conducted in order to assist you in preparing a draft for the Secretary-General?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I cannot give you either yes or no. I simply do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could have one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, in cooperation -- I will see what Mr. Hedaraly uses in his cross-examination and rather than taking him through additional code cables, I will sit down with Mr. Hedaraly and see if we can bar table remaining code cables into evidence, whatever he doesn't use in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And with that, thank you very much, Mr. Akashi. I have concluded my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. Mr. Akashi, we will have a break, but before we adjourn for that, could I inquire with the other Defence teams how much time they would need for the cross-examinations of Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I anticipate I will be under one session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under one session. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, depending on what happens in front much me, I may be half a session at most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Half a session at most. And then, Mr. Hedaraly, I'm turning to you, what could we expect from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Less than one session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Less than one session. Mr. Akashi, this leads it my conclusion that we most likely will not finish today but very likely finish somewhere tomorrow morning. We will first have a break. We will resume at five minutes to 11.00. And, Mr. Kay, already to inform you, the next break will start at 12.20. We'd like to see you back in -- at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Much obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just waiting to see if I can see Mr. Akashi. Yes. Hello, Mr. Akashi, I'm asking you some questions now on behalf of Mr. Cermak. My name is Steven Kay. The first matter I would like ask to you look at and consider is a document we have called D28. It's in tab 1 of the file. And if you could just look at this document, Mr. Akashi, and you might --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- remember it. It was the agreement signed by you and Mr. Sarinic. On page 2 of the document, you'll see your signature.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recollect this document?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this was the document for the temporary measures to be applied in Sectors North and Sector South; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the intention of the agreement was to deal with the revised status or mandate of UNCRO in the liberated areas of Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This document was signed by you and Mr. Sarinic on the 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it set out the new relationship between UNCRO and the government of Croatia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that previously the areas that you had been upon with UNCRO, as part of the RSK territory, had now changed in their status and the role of UNCRO had changed?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I cannot make comment on -- on your statement as to whether our mandate with regard to Croatia has -- has completely changed or not, but certainly the situation has undergone some transformation. Therefore, our tasks became somewhat different. But I'm not an international lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Looking at the document, paragraph 2, because you probably need your memory refreshing, deals with the monitoring of the human rights situation and giving the right of information -- intervention to UNCRO and other agencies, when appropriate. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And just taking these -- a couple of the issues from the document. Paragraph 3, concerning another issue about allowing the previous inhabitants to remain peacefully; Croatia allowing, with full guarantees for security, departure from those areas of all those expressing their desire to do so, with exception to those who committed violations of international criminal law.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And in paragraph 4 on page 2 of the document, full access by UNCRO and humanitarian organisations, specifying UNHCR, ICRC, to the civilian population for the purpose of providing for the humanitarian needs of that population.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "This will be assured by the Croatian authorities to the extent allowed by objective security considerations." And then in paragraph 5, UNMOs, human rights monitoring elements of UNCRO "will carry out surveillance immediately in all areas except where, in the opinion of the local UNCRO military commanders after consulting Croatian Army commanders, the security situation does not permit for such surveillance." That's all I need to look at in the document at this stage, and I've done it to refresh your memory. I want to ask you --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- this: Was this an already-prepared document that you had, or was it one put together after the 5th August and the Croatian military offensive had been successful?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, my notes indicate that I had two meetings with Mr. Sarinic on the 5th of August, and in those meetings I raised a matter of agreeing with the Croatian government on a host of human rights majors. And this agreement signed on the 6th of August, the following day, is one of the products of those discussions in the previous day, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In relation to this document that Mr. Sarinic had signed, did you discuss with him at all the legal status of this agreement within Croatia?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I cannot be very specific, but I, myself, being an international civil servant with political science background rather than with international law background, I thought it's incumbent with my responsibility to sign this kind of document at the earliest possible opportunity so that we can save some lives and alleviate the suffering of IDPs and refugees. So these pragmatic considerations prepared myself and my colleagues to sign this type of agreement. It is -- we were not very much concerned about the legal or legalistic character of such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, and I accept your answer in respect of that. In relation to Mr. Sarinic, did you know what his authority was to sign such agreement?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no doubt on my mind that Mr. Sarinic had requisite authority to sign such a document. He's -- he's a man I have dealt with, I have respected, and I knew that he had the full confidence of President Tudjman. He was always efficient, and so no doubt existed in my mind that he had full authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know what his position and job was?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was chef de cabinet of President Tudjman, so far as I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Any other job or position that he may have had in the government; did you know if he had any job there?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that he had some other positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to this agreement, then, signed with Mr. Sarinic, was there any reason why you didn't sign it with President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That question did not come up to my mind. I had occasional meetings with President Tudjman himself, but in most cases, Mr. Sarinic acted in full power on behalf of the Croatian government. He was always very business-like and he acted with considerable confidence, and in no occasion was I in doubt that he had less than full authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to the terms of this agreement, do you know how it was intended to be implemented by Mr. Sarinic?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had confidence that the full agreement will be carried out in good faith by both parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning now to another document which arises from the 7th of August of 1995. If that could be put before you, tab 2. And in that document, if we turn to the page with the stamp 908. And I will ask you some general questions about this document before we look at the content of it. Mr. Akashi, the document you're looking at --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- are the notes of a man called Mr. Bambury who, I believe, acted as an assistant to you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Tony Bambury was one of the young, very bright, very effective assistants of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And after signing the agreement on the 6th of August, you went on the 7th of August to Knin to see for yourself --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- the situation in that town; is that right?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you recollect how you travelled to Knin?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay. I -- my notes indicate that I left Zagreb at 7.45 a.m., and I had a stopover in Split, and I arrived in Knin at 10.00 a.m. I think all my travels were by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the reason you didn't travel by road because of the security situation at that time?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Kay. I think it was because helicopter is the most convenient and very rapid means of transportation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The page we're looking at now, 908, is series of notes written by Mr. Bambury on that day regarding your activities, and can you see in the middle of the page: Knin, Sector South headquarters, HQ, and the date. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it records a briefing. Was that a briefing in the UNCRO camp in Knin as to what had happened in the previous two days or three days?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one second, please. I should think, yeah, this briefing, this concerns note made by Tony Bambury on the briefing given to us on the 7th of August in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we go now to the next page, 909.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can see on line 3: "In the past the ARSK never available to meet us, wanted emergency meeting/assistance to evac 32.000." Do you recollect being told that that was the situation faced by UNCRO, that the RSK leadership had asked for the evacuation of 32.000 Serbs from the region?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not specifically recall discussion on -- on -- on this particular matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The note being into Mr. Bambury's notebook in that form, would you find it being a reliable note, something that you would rely on?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would rely on Mr. Bambury, but I'm not sure whether I would rely on notes made by Tony Bambury in all instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we then move through the document. Next page, 6910. And we see in the middle of the page, and if I'm saying anything that is unreasonable or unusual, please, anyone, interrupt, but I will say meeting with General Cermak, 7th of August, is what the note indicates. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And just for the notice of the Court and the record, I intend to do that. I hope that that is an acceptable way of dealing with the evidence, and if I've got anything wrong, please interrupt, but I think it's better for the record and more efficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Seems to meet no objections by Mr. Hedaraly, neither by the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that's correct, there was a meeting between you, a man called Mr. Min, other people, including Mr. Hussein, General Forand, a Mr. Armstrong, with General Cermak and five Croatian military, plus some civilians. Do you recollect that?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have specific recollection of that meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but I remember some of the names mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recollect that at that meeting you presented a copy of the agreement signed the previous day between you and Mr. Sarinic to General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall showing a copy of the agreement to General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We see from the note that General Cermak said that the agreement would be respected. Do you recollect that?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you requested "freedom of movement for our military and civilian staff," and you referred in the agreement for the UNMOs and human rights "folks," is the word, to monitor the situation? Do you recollect having a meeting with General Cermak and discussing that?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Indeed, my notes made at that time indicated that I had a meeting with General Cermak, and he was quite cooperative. He acted efficiently. And after the meeting, two of us had a press conference, and -- yes. Then I met with 800 refugees, who are very happy to see me visit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll just look at the content of this note and to see if you can recollect or deal with any of the issues contained within Mr. Bambury's notes. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But before we do, that I'd like to give an opportunity to Mr. Hedaraly who is on his feet to address us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I don't know if the record was clear enough that the last answer of the witness when he referred to "my notes made at the time," he was also looking at the note -- his diary or what he had brought with him in the room when he gave his answers, and not to be confused with the notes of Mr. Bambury, based on the Court's previous guidance. I just wanted to make that clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, when you referred to the note, you referred to your personal notes that you were consulting, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, My Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we continue, Mr. Kay, you briefly mentioned who would have been present during this meeting. Then the name of a Mr. Armstrong came up, a full text search doesn't show any Mr. Armstrong until now, and it is not in my recollection. May I take it that you interpreted JA as referring to a Mr. Armstrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Almstrom, A-l-m-s-t-r-o-m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That may explain why --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Almstrom, A-l-m-s-t-r-o-m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then this being clarified, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn to page 6911 of the Bambury notes, and we have a note here of Mr. Cermak agreeing with that, "concerning the freedom of movement. Wasn't able to earlier because of security reasons, which you understand from this point on get your liaison officer to contact the Croatian military liaison officer and everything will be done through normal channels." First of all, do you recollect a discussion on those lines?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a recollection of specific contents of these discussions, but, I had, as I told you a meeting with Mr. -- General Cermak, and these were matters within the purview of our concern during that visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where we see the reference to normal channels and the liaison officers, are you able to explain in any way what that means?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, we had a presence in Knin, and there were military officers as well as several civilians. And by normal channels, my guess is that these are the people who serve as normal channels of communication between the Croatians -- Croatian officials and the United Nations side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on in that page, there's discussion about the essential services in Knin. We've no need to look at that. But we see on the bottom four lines you refer to the 799 refugees in the compound "and need to find ways to help them leave." And Mr. Cermak --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- said: "Everyone can leave the camp, go to their homes, take things from their homes, hope they'll remain in Knin. Hope very much they'll stay but won't do anything to prevent them leaving." And the rest of the text can be read. I won't waste time. Is it correct, you recollect that, discussing the future of the people who had gone to the UNCRO camp in Knin?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have specific recollection of discussing these questions with General Cermak, but this note of the meeting seems to indicate that, indeed, such a discussion did take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Turning now onto that page, 6912, further down into the middle of the paragraph: "People are moving freely in the town. Give personal assurances for security. All our contacts will be humane. You will see it." Do you recollect General Cermak being supportive of the need for people to be secure in Knin and to be treated humanely?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recollect that his general attitude was supportive. He was agreeable, and he seemed to be very responsive to our requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Further on that page, we see he refers to a medical team that had "come from Zadar yesterday." Do you recollect discussion about a Croatian medical team in Knin?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have specific recollection in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
