utterances.text: At the foot of that page, you refer to the Croatian government and UN in full agreement. If we turn to 6913, the next page, and you refer to "full protection, human rights, and concrete measures taking to calm the situation."

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would this be an accurate portrayal, as far as you think, of the meeting between you and Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be very specific, but such discussion seems to be in conformity with the atmosphere of our meeting with General Cermak that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the middle of that page, he says: "We'll do everything also to help them, to clean and repair houses. Tomorrow we'll open up a welfare office for the civilian population." And you state --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And then you state: "For those who want to leave, despite our efforts, need to give full guarantees for safe departure?"

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "Well established procedure for screening those who want to leave. We're ready to start monitoring human rights situation."

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "Want your cooperation" --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- et cetera.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: About this statement, may I ask you this question: Was it already in the mind of the United Nations, UNCRO, and other organisations that, in fact, a large proportion of the Serbian population intended to leave Croatia?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I cannot answer your question, but it must have been on our mind that some Serb population who are still in Knin, some of them may wish, indeed, to leave Knin for other destinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was the well-established procedure for screening those who want to leave? Can you recollect what that was and explain it?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was referring to the established procedures which UNHCR apply, to ascertain two wishes of the people, to stay or to leave, to make sure that there's full consent on the part of people concerned as to their movements. And I do not know the details of such procedures, but HCR applies these procedures in many other places as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Akashi. Would that be an informed consent that they were making in relation to their request to leave?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should think that that is informed consent. But I'm not sure what -- what definition you give to "informed consent."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn to the next page, 6914.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Cermak is referring to having his guarantees for movement. "People can go to houses and move freely." And then there was a problem concerning -- within the camp, "50 or 70 military that will have to pass procedures of interview with our civilian police." Do you recollect that particular issue concerning RSK soldiers having also been in the UNCRO camp with civilians?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection of discussion of this particular question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recollect in the agreement that you and Mr. Sarinic signed that, in fact, there was within one of those clauses acknowledgment of the fact that the Croatian government had the right to detain those suspected of war crimes? It's in paragraph 3 of the Akashi-Sarinic agreement, Exhibit D28. It's a document the Court is well familiar with, Mr. Akashi, before your arrival.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, exception being made for those had committed violations of international criminal law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we can see here, you requested a presence throughout the legal process.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And Mr. Cermak said you can be sure of that. Must liaise with the deputy minister of the interior and ensure that everything goes well.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recollect the discussion about the procedure for those concerning the Croatians [sic] who may have committed war crimes?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not specifically recall, but I think in the course of discussion of this kind, these questions are raised, and I think General Cermak was fully cooperative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move to page 915. Mr. Cermak refers to two doctors being with him. And we see further down the page you mentioned that HCR was ready to send humanitarian aid convoys to Knin, and Mr. Cermak saying, No problem. And we can see that he would like to address the detained persons as well. Do you recollect that --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- discussion?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specific recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it seem to be accord with the substance of what was being discussed between you and him on 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It seems to be in general accord to the tenure of -- tone of our discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We turn to page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, before we move to the next page about the doctors, the last two words, perhaps you could put to the witness -- I read them as "not military," but -- the second entry on the page, "Cermak have two doctors with me." That portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last two words of that section read --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "Medical care up to doctors, not military."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, "not military."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask the witness. Mr. Akashi, could you tell us, have you read that portion of the notes? Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On page 915.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection as what "not military" means in this context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I have no recollection as to what specifically this phrase was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we just turn to page 9916, we see there Mr. Almstrom's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, were you put some further questions to Mr. Akashi in relation to Mr. Almstrom, because where I didn't find Armstrong, I neither find Almstrom on the transcript of the whole of case, so he is a new person for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could you inform us as to who Mr. Almstrom was and what his role within the UN was at that time?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would be glad to. John Almstrom was in my own cabinet. He was from Canadian military service with considerably more experiences of the former Yugoslavia than myself, and he was one of the hardest working persons I ever met in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm sure he is very grateful, if he's listening, to hear that. In relation to the conversation at this stage, Mr. Almstrom was raising the issue of interviewing males of military age and that the procedures should be handled carefully; otherwise, it contributes to pressure on people to leave. Do you recollect that particular concern of the UN at that time?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- I have no specifically recollection of this conversation. But it is in accord with the general tenure of our discussion and our concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we can see Mr. Almstrom said that people had been brought from the Centre of Human Rights who would be -- who could help set up procedures. First of all, the Centre for Human Rights, can you explain the context of that group and what they were doing in Knin then?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that John Almstrom was referring to field personnel from the Office of High Commissioner for human rights residing in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cermak said: "We will arrange a meeting between your human rights people and my headquarters tomorrow. Headquarters Knin will always be open to you. I want everyone to be aware of our complying with human rights." Does that reflect the attitude of General Cermak when you met him?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn to the next page, 6917 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I'm still a bit struggling with those present. You read that Mr. Hussein was present from the testimony of Mr. Hussein Al-Alfi, it comes to my mind that Mr. Hussein may actually be Mr. Hussein Al-Alfi. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is our understanding. It is Mr. Al-Alfi that is referring to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise, Your Honour, for not taking that more slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's clear. His testimony also includes that he -- I think that he fetched Mr. Akashi from the helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Landing spot. Well now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have we answered the question correctly, Mr. Akashi, as to Mr. Hussein being Mr. Al-Alfi?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this name of Mr. Hussein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember the name Al-Alfi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That -- could you give me some more information about him? The name seems to ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could he be the civilian coordinator in the area at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah, yes. In that case, he was -- he was a very agreeable colleague of mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could it have been that he was present during this meeting with General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not absolutely sure. I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Moving to page 6917, we can see there's further agreement there, and then Brigadier General Forand is referred to in the middle of the page. Do you recollect him as the commander of UN Sector South?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And he stated: "Want freedom of movement total and not have it disappear" from when you leave essentially; SRSG leaves? Do you recollect him saying that?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recollect General Cermak referring to the fact that: "Areas had to be seen to be safe for freedom of movement and that from tomorrow you should be able to move in most of my area of responsibility, including Knin town. If you have any problems, please, see me personally." Do you recollect that?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specific conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn to the next page, 6918, do you recollect the Croatian Army legal officer -- liaison officer, sorry. Liaison officer, intervening after General Cermak had spoke -- not doing very well at the moment, am I? Can I rephrase that. After General Cermak had spoken, did you realise that -- did you recollect that the Croatian Army liaison officer intervened to express --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... point of view.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recollect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There was an issue that required that: "Continuation of UN operations in the area will be discussed by the Croatian Ministry of Defence. Giving freedom of movement doesn't mean can you have random visits for anywhere?" Do you recollect that?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And then Mr. Cermak stating: "We're not talking about such larger issues?" Do you remember him addressing the liaison officer as to his comments?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We've no need to go into any further detail on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we move to 6919.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: General Cermak stated: "We've issued orders for the Croatian military to withdraw from Knin and some other towns. Only civilian and military police can enter Knin. All roads will be blocked, and no one will enter without my permission." Do you recollect him stating that?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no specific recollection of these remarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And then on that page we see a CIVREPCRO, civilian representative of Croatia, a Dr. Lang. Do you recollect a Dr. Slobodan Lang being president -- being present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know Dr. Lang?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't -- I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see what the record says about his statement. If we turn to the next page, 6920 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, if there's any thing we're supposed to read from that, you have been most helpful in deciphering the short language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if there's any specific portion you would like to draw our attention to, I would invite you to read it so that all parties understand how you read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The last three lines: "Regardless of ethnic origin, all equal citizens of Croatia, large numbers left because of misinformation and propaganda." I hope that assists the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go on to page 6920, you referred to there being a press conference. And do you recollect that you described your talks as being cordial with General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was generally very cordial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. The passage I want to ask you about is right in the middle.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "As of tomorrow, UN and other agencies will have freedom of movement in and around Knin. Day after, larger areas depending on security. Agreed together to make maximum appeal to people to stay. Reassure people, nothing to be afraid of ... but if want to go, go in security." It's the area on freedom of movement that I wanted to draw your attention to, that in your discussions with General Cermak, did you express this correctly, that, as of tomorrow - that would be the 8th of August - UN and other agencies will have freedom of movement in and around Knin, and the day after --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recollect that? I'll stop there.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall specifics, but this is in accord with the general thrust of our discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that the day after "larger areas, depending on security," which would be the 9th of August.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I do not recall specifics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would it be correct to consider this matter as one in which security of the region played a significant role in relation to where the freedom of movement was to be?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we turn to page 6922, do you recollect one of the journalists at the press conference saying to you: "All people we spoke to want to leave and are afraid they won't be able to. Will the United Nations help them to leave?" And your reply --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "UN will help in accordance with well-established procedures for establishing free will."

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not -- I do not recall specific exchanges at the press conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could just turn to page 6925, you'll see on line 6 something that I -- I put to you earlier about the informed choice, that that was your position, if people decided to leave.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As being one of your expressions; that's where I got it from.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I look quite well-informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you I have no further questions. Make this document be made an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D1667.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1667 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kuzmanovic. Mr. Kuzmanovic is counsel for Mr. Markac, and I'll keep a close eye on the clock here. We'll have a break there 20 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Hopefully I will be done by then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You were asked some questions, Mr. Akashi, about and presented some documents regarding the shelling that occurred, or damage from shelling in Knin, and at the time you said you were in Sarajevo during Operation Storm; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When -- during the operation -- military operation in Sector West, I was in Sarajevo, yes. I mean, at the outset.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean Sectors North and South or Sector West meaning Western Slavonia? Are you talking about Knin or are you talking about Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Western Slavonia is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the operation which commenced --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: In May of 1995?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 1st of May, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you when Operation Storm began?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you have been to Sarajevo, you stated, on many occasions?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you been to Vukovar in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And when you walked in Knin, you would agree with me, Mr. Akashi, that Knin was nothing remotely resembling Vukovar or Sarajevo, correct, in terms of damage?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukovar was really -- the destruction was so complete that it -- it could not be compared to conditions I found in other cities. I -- I -- I would not dare to make easy comparisons. Destruction of any city is very painful to watch. But the extent of damage of Vukovar was beyond anything which a normal human being would have experienced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you agree with me, Mr. Akashi, that the destruction that you saw in Sarajevo, as well, could not compare in any remote fashion with what you observed in Knin after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure whether I would use the adjective "remote." But I think Sarajevo's destruction was larger than the destruction I witnessed in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like, Mr. Registrar, to please pull up 65 ter 3D00900. And for the Court's reference and for all in the courtroom, this is a report from Helsinki Watch dated July 1995 of the Croatian military operation in Western Slavonia. Unfortunately, we don't have a translation of this yet. We just received this yesterday, uploaded it into e-court. It's in English, and we will, obviously, have the relevant portions that I'm going to refer to translated, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then I take it that the Prosecution will have an opportunity to comment on whether more portions should be translated and whether more portions are relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, I'd like to refer to you page 2 of the document -- of this particular document and the bottom --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Your Honour, I got it yesterday so it's not in the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- could you please look at your screen because there's no hard copy of this document available in Tokyo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And my apologies to you, Mr. Akashi, for not having this earlier. We received this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Could counsel please repeat the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Page 2 at the bottom, the sentence beginnings, "Many Serbs."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Before I ask the question relating to this document, Mr. Akashi, you were asked some questions about the exodus of the Serb population in Western Slavonia and also the exodus of the Serb position in Sectors North and South after Operation Storm. This particular Helsinki Watch report discusses what happened in -- in part in Sector West in Western Slavonia, and I will read the portion of this report and then I'll ask you a question or two about it. At the bottom of page 2 the report states: "Many Serbs who remained in Western Slavonia after the offensive have left for Serb-controlled territory in Bosnia or Croatia, and the vast majority of the remaining Serbs have expressed their wish to leave, claiming there is little chance of peaceful co-existence between Serbs and Croat, particularly with those Croats who were displaced from their homes by Serbian forces in 1991 and will now be returning to Western Slavonia." Mr. Akashi, it's true, is it not, based on your experience, both in Western Slavonia and in Sector South, that Serb populations who left these areas were repopulated in either Eastern Slavonia, meaning in the area in and around Vukovar, in Serb-occupied parts of Bosnia or even in Kosovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question again, please, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. No problem, Mr. Akashi. Based on your experience as the Special Representative of the Secretary-General, in Western Slavonia and in Sectors North and South, the Serb populations who left were -- were repopulated in many areas or repatriated in Eastern Slavonia, in Serb-occupied parts of Bosnia and even in places like Kosovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That was the policy, at least, of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to remove and repopulate these populations who had left; correct?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I'm not sure whether it was a specific policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's, in fact, though in practice what had happened; correct?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I would imagine so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 12 of that report, please. Thank you, Mr. Monkhouse, for your assistance in Tokyo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And on page 12 of the report, before the footnotes begin, the paragraph that begins: "Some Serbs who fled from Western Slavonia to northern Bosnia have been resettled in parts of Eastern Slavonia, another Serbian-controlled area of Croatia. As a result, Croats have left or been expelled from the villages of the Bapska and Tovarnik in Eastern Slavonia, suggesting that Serbs from Western Slavonia may have been resettled in the Croats' homes?" Now, Mr. Akashi, at least according to the Helsinki Watch report, the experience from Western Slavonia was that when the Serbian population left, it was resettled in areas, for example, in Eastern Slavonia; correct?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no means to ascertain whether that statement is correct or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This particular section of report states: "During the fighting on May 1-2, an estimated 5000 to 7500 Serbs fled Western Slavonia for Bosnian Serb-held regions. More have since fled, and most were initially taken to the Bosnian Serb-held city of Banja Luka in north-western Bosnia. According to UNHCR officials, many of the arriving Serbian refugees are heavily armed, and since their arrival, a series of attacks on Catholic churches and monasteries in the Banja Luka area have taken place." Now, were you privy to UNHCR reports, Mr. Akashi?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection of reports on this particular question from UNHCR or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. If you look down below, Mr. Akashi, on the same page in footnote 33 of this particular report, there's an indication that UNHCR officials that were interviewed by Human Rights Watch representatives discussed the amount of Serbian refugees who were resettled; for example, 2500 were resettled in Bosanski Brod, 1500 in Derventa, and others resettled in Eastern Slavonia which was called another Serbian-controlled area in Croatia. Do you recall -- have any specific recollection of the repopulation of Serbian refugees who have left Western Slavonia into other Serb-populated areas of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, I have no recollection of having heard or read such UNHCR reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to go to page 5 of the report, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Page 5 of the report, Mr. Akashi --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: -- generally discusses UNPROFOR, its role, and the UN's role specifically in Croatia. And in the middle of the page in the paragraph that says, "Despite": "Despite its three-year-long presence in the UNPAs, UNPROFOR has failed to fulfil any part of its mandate." Instead of reading this entire paragraph, I wanted to talk to you just generally about your role, in terms of the United Nations role. Would you agree with me that at least as of May 1, 1995, the United Nations failed in its mission with regard to the UN Protected Areas?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is important not to reach a hasty conclusion as the role played by the United Nations in the UNPAs. You see, in Croatia, UN did play a positive role, in that, at least its presence prevented the resumption of fighting, and it served to maintain a precarious cease-fire. Certainly the other part of its mandate was not fulfilled, in the sense of disarmament to be achieved in these UNPAs. So you can look at it as a bottle half-filled. You may be dissatisfied about the emptiness of it, but if you look at it from the other side, it is still one-half filled --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- so it depends on your expectations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, would you agree with me that repatriation of non-Serbs in Serb-held areas was one of the goals that the UN failed to do in the UNPAs?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in that task UN did not accomplish its objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to go to page 1 of the report -- actually, page 2, I'm sorry. 1 is the cover sheet. The second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The second paragraph reads: "In an unfortunate and premature assessment, UN officials - most notably Yasushi Akashi, the Secretary-General's Special Representative to the former Yugoslavia - alleged that 'massive' human rights abuses by Croatian authorities had taken place during the offensive. Evidence of wide spread abuse has not emerges, however; the information available at the time was flawed, incomplete and required further investigation and corroboration." Mr. Akashi, I want to ask you specifically about this section of the report. What prompted you to allege that massive human rights abuses were committed in Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not able to answer this question, unless my statements are placed in the full context of the statements actually made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, can you explain to us why you aren't able to comment?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot respond to partial quotations of remarks that I may have made. Everything has to be interpreted contextually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, Mr. Misetic went through with you several documents relating to houses burned, and one of the figures was 22.000 houses were burned, allegedly, after Operation Storm. Now, if true, if there were 22.000 houses burned that's -- would be considered a pretty massive human rights violation, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yet in not one single cable, coded written cable report to Kofi Annan in August/September or October of 1995 is any figure mentioned other than 200, in terms of houses burned; correct? Is that correct, Mr. Akashi?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which report are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the reports that Mr. Misetic went through with you, those coded reports, cables that went to Mr. Annan, Kofi Annan. You didn't mention any of those figures of 22.000 houses or 16.000 houses or however many houses --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a cable but a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Security Council report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Or cables, correct? Either one.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is one of the Security Council reports, which was not as specific as you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you can't recall, as we sit here today, whether you brought this up to Mr. Sarinic in any of your meetings, according to what you told Mr. Misetic; correct?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: One more question, Your Honour, and then I'm done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One more question then, that's fine, because I committed myself to a break at 12.20. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi you would agree with me that a figure of 22.000 burned houses is flawed, incomplete, or required further investigation or corroboration; correct?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to move the portions that we referenced of this report into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we deal with that after the break, if you wouldn't mind so that we know exactly which portions are tendered into evidence and which -- of which portions we expect translations. Mr. Akashi, we will have a break --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and we resume in half an hour from now, which is our local time, a quarter to 1.00, which may be quarter to 8.00 in your local time, if ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's 7.30 p.m. in Tokyo time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then our clocks are a bit different. But in a half-hour from this very moment, we'd like to see you back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Court would forgive me, there is a correction in the transcript that I'm sure that all parties will understand at page 49, line 19, it's got "concerning the Croatians who may have committed." It's concerning the suspected war crimes actually was the phrase I used. The Court will be aware of this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what exactly would be the correction, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Concerning, I said the suspected war criminals was my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- at this moment, I really --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's concerning the Croatians, and it's the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say the ... well it will be checked. I have no clear recollection and in view of the answer, I take it that I would not expect Mr. Akashi to have a different recollection, even if would you have phrased the question in a -- a different way because he certainly would have drawn our attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- that will be verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kuzmanovic you would like to tender your --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Before I wanted to do that, I just wanted to thank Mr. Akashi and the Registrar's representative in Tokyo for dealing with the document the way we did, and it was very efficient and helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You wanted to tender the Helsinki Watch July 1995 report which we have in English only at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Hedaraly, have you checked with Mr. Kuzmanovic the portions --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I have not check with the Mr. Kuzmanovic. But it may make more sense to have the whole report. There was many sections that were jumped and for the full context, the whole report can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the report will be exhibit D1668.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1668 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for your information, we will make sure that the entire document gets translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Mr. Akashi will you now be cross-examined by Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will now be cross-examined by Mr. Hedaraly. Mr. Hedaraly is counsel for the Prosecution in this case. Mr. Hedaraly, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. First I want to go back on a topic that up was discussed yesterday which is your meeting with the Krajina leadership in Knin on 30 July 1995. And you will recall some questions from Mr. Misetic regarding whether there was or was not an agreement with Mr. Martic and others, and the following letter that you sent to President Tudjman, if you recall that discussion yesterday.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can first have Exhibit D1653 on the screen here and that will be, Mr. Registrar, in Tokyo, tab 5 of the Gotovina Defence binder, I believe. If you would confirm that for me, I would be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Could counsel please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: D1653. It's a 1 August cable sent by Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, I have tab 5 in the Gotovina Defence binder, 65 ter 1D1586. That's an a coded cable dated 1st August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is correct. And that is Exhibit D1653. Thank you, Mr. Monkhouse.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And I wanted to go page 5 paragraph 13m and you were read a portion of this paragraph yesterday and now I want to read the end of it to you, specifically the last sentence, where you stated: "I then made comments to the press to the effect that I had received explicit assurances from Martic that the RSK authorities considered themselves bound by the full terms of the document, and that I considered them similarly bound." Now, before I ask you my question, let me also show a video-clip of that press meeting and we will show it, if you look on your screen, we will show it via Sanction; that is 65 ter 1D2680.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, it's a Defence video. We don't have the transcript. It only one minute and Mr. Akashi speaks fairly slowly in it, so we can replay it again if necessary for the court reporter and the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we will see whether the interpreters exceptionally will be able to work without the transcript. Let's give it a try. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: "Yasushi Akashi: After five hours and a half of very arduous and non-stop discussions and negotiations in Knin, I was able to get the agreement of the Krajina leadership, consisting of Mr. Martic, Mr. Babic, and General Markasic to the text of our agreement consisting of six points, and this agreement is of great importance in view of extremely tense and dangerous situation in which this ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I have stopped the video here just for the sake of my question. If you want to watch the full clip, it's under two minutes, let me know. But my question for you is: Based on the portion of the cable I wrote to you and based on the video where you stated that you received the agreement of Mr. Martic and others, did you, in fact, consider that you had reached such agreement with the Krajina leadership, despite the behaviour of Mr. Martic and Mr. Macura at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. Martic agreed with us to observe these six points during our meeting. However, as I told you yesterday and is described in my cable to New York, he changed -- he apparently changed his mind, and he decided to backtrack on that, and we were extremely disappointed and disturbed by his sudden change of attitude. I think his colleagues who are with him were also taken by surprise, and, therefore, we wanted to tell the entire press that there was an agreement at some point in time, and then there were subsequent change of mind by Mr. Martic. So I wanted everybody to know that there was agreement; then by some emotional turn of events, only one person in the Knin leadership felt that he could not honour it, he did not want to honour it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Akashi, for that answer. And when you say he backtracked or did not want to honour it, that's the reference that we saw yesterday to him refusing to sign the document; correct?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hedaraly. The covering letter of my cable is carefully phrased to indicate these developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can turn to tab 19 of the Prosecution binder, for the Registrar in -- in Tokyo. And it will be 65 ter 7401 for the e-court system here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And this is a cable -- another cable from you, dated 7 August to Mr. Annan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And I would like to go to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if you look at the third full paragraph, which says -- don't have it on the screen yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't believe that the documents have been released in e-court to the Defence yet. So if we can ask that they be released to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, don't worry, this is a technical matter in our e-court system which was raised by Mr. Misetic. It will be resolved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If you have it in front of you, Mr. Akashi, the third full paragraph --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... which starts: "My special representative held emergency talks on 30 July with the local Serb authorities in Knin" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have it on the e-court screen either, so if we could wait until we could actually follow along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's see whether ... I think we have it on our screen now. Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The third full paragraph on the second page of that cable which essentially summarises what had occurred the previous week. In that paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Hedaraly. Your Honour we don't have it on our screens here, and I can't seem to find -- there we go. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me try it one more time, Mr. Akashi. "My Special Representative held emergency talks on 30 July with the local Serb authorities in Knin. He secured a six-point commitment from the Krajina Serbs that the ARSK would withdraw fully from the Bihac pocket and desist from further cross-border interference (see Annex A)," which is the six-point text. And let me also show you 65 ter 7398, which is tab 16 of the same binder, which is a 3 August cable. Where at this time, if we go to the second page -- do we have it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We're having some technical difficulties, Mr. Akashi, but my question for you -- it was another cable that dealt with the word commitment by the Krajina leadership. Hopefully we can resolve it and show it to you soon. My question was: There you referred to commitment. We saw agreement. We heard your answer that -- that Mr. Martic backtracked, refused to sign it, and I'm just trying to get some -- some clarity in -- what was your understanding of what the situation was at the end of that meeting, although he refused to sign it? What did you understand the situation to be?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The end of the meeting, as I recall it, was somewhat confusing, and the confused. After a long negotiations and very serious talks, arguments, counter-arguments, at some point in time, we were able to extract agreement of Mr. Martic on six important matters, and this was observed by his colleagues on the civilian side, as well as on the military side, by RSK. And then -- and the negotiations continued -- actually continued for over five hours, and in the end, we left the meeting at about 4.30 p.m., and no time for lunch. And Mr. Martic, somehow, had a sudden change of mind, and the -- originally we discussed and agreed to go before the press to show that agreement had, indeed, been reached. Therefore, sort of a defusing the atmosphere of impending crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank -- I'm sorry, I thought you were finished, but if you want to finish your answer, please do so.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In effect, I wanted to describe a rather unusual atmosphere of that meeting, where there were, sort of sudden changes of atmosphere. But at some point in time, we were certain that there was a set of assurances given to us when they were all clear-headed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If can I tender 65 ter 1D2680 and 65 ter 7401 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter number 1D2680 will be Exhibit P2626; and 65 ter number 7401 will be Exhibit P2627.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2626 and P2627 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, we saw yesterday also your correspondence of the evening of 30th of July with President Tudjman. I don't want to discuss them, but if you want to see them, we can. I want to focus on the following day. Were you aware that that day, the 31st of July, President Tudjman met with military advisors to discuss a military operation against the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was ignorant of those meetings which you refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you at tab 3 of the Prosecution binder, which is P461. And if we go to the first page of the English, also first page of the B/C/S. In that meeting it starts: "The president addresses the meeting." And the second paragraph -- I will wait for it to come up on the screen here before reading the portion to you. Thank you. And it reads: "As you know, we were determined to undertake further operations. The Grahovo-Glamoc operation was also designed to have an impact with respect to Bihac and to enable Knin to be surrounded. We were determined to start lifting the blockade of Bihac from the west. "However, the situation as it stands now, is that the UN representatives, Akashi, Stoltenberg, and the Serbs have deprived us of this reason, since they are in the process of withdrawing their forces from the Bihac area." For the next paragraph, the next page in the B/C/S: "Accordingly, we no longer have the necessary justification to lift the blockade of Bihac." And the next paragraph again: "Therefore, it is my opinion that our main objective can no longer be to break through to Bihac." Now if we can just jump ahead to page 32, which is the next-to-last page, and it is page 62 in the B/C/S. Just to be clear for everyone in the meantime. What you had discussed with the Krajina leadership the six points, part of that discussion was related to the situation in Bihac; correct?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you said the middle here again where the president talks. It starts with the main problem with UNCRO, with those Japanese bugs. Do you see that portion?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The problem will be with UNCRO with those Japanese bugs. It is their proposal, Akashi argued it with them for five hours and then submitted proposal that UNCRO would deploy towards Bihac to stop us and would place observers on Dinara. There is then an intervention from the minister of defence, Mr. Susak, which ends with, I wouldn't go to Geneva and President Tudjman responds, Hold on, I'm going to Geneva to hide this and not to talk. I won't send a minister but the assistant foreign minister. That's on Thursday. "So I want to hide what we are preparing for the day after. And we can rebut any argument in the world about how we didn't want to talk, but that we only wanted what ..." Now, Mr. Akashi, in your statement to the Gotovina Defence at paragraph 5, you described President Tudjman as a reliable negotiator. Now when you said that, you were not aware of this passage I just read to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And -- well, actually, let me deal with this while we're on the same topic. You also described Mr. Sarinic in your statement as a reliable and professional negotiator; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Mr. Akashi, did Mr. Sarinic ever, in front of you, refer to the Serbs as being a cancer in the stomach of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, if he had referred to Serbs as a cancer in the stomach of Croatia, or you had come to learn that he referred to the Serbs as a cancer in the stomach of Croatia, that would have affected your opinion of him as reliable and professional negotiator; correct?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment on this. I -- my judgement of people I'm dealing with is based on the totality of their personality, their character, their integrity, their consistency, and all these factors. I'm not influenced by any specific words or remarks. Sometimes all of us make slip of tongue, and so my -- I will not be able to give you a categorical answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Akashi. Thank you for your answer. There was a reference is to Geneva. Do you remember the details of what precisely transpired in those negotiations in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, to save time, I would propose to bar table 65 ter 1D1593, which is a note by Mr. Stoltenberg who was -- I know that Geneva negotiations were discussed a few times here. I would just propose to bar table so the Chamber has the note of the person that was there. There is no point in asking questions about it to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if i could have an opportunity to review. We've just been released these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That was one of the Defence exhibits for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that is the case, that comes as a surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear him say it was a 1D number, so I'm sorry, Mr. President. Yes, then obviously I was going to bar table these as well as I indicated at the close of my direct, so it's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 1D1593 would receive number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is will be Exhibit P2628.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence from the bar table. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, we have been discussing here a number of your coded cables that you sent, and I just want everyone to - including myself - to understand exactly the process how these were prepared. So I just wanted to ask you, first of all, when you sent those cables, and I understand from yesterday that you did not necessarily draft them yourself, what was the source of the information that was contained in those cables?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, would you specify what cable or cables you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Sure, I apologise for that. The cables that you would send to Mr. Annan, the type of cables we have been seeing yesterdays and today sent from yourself to Mr. Annan reporting on various aspects of what was occurring.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to cables describing my meetings with President Tudjman, Mr. Sarinic, and other leaders I was negotiating with, then, even if the first draft was drafted by one of my colleagues, I carefully reviewed every word of it; and I made necessary changes, if needed, and then, only then, I signed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And this is for your meetings and negotiations, I understand. With respect to other cables reporting, for example, crimes that occurred or reports that the UN was getting of human rights violations, what -- what source of information would you rely on in these types of cables?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, there were information sent to us by UN Military Observers deployed to many different areas. In those cases, we transmitted their reports and the findings to headquarters without our attempting to make changes or amendments. These were, by their very nature, factual reports. The same applies to reports by human rights observers and teams. They were prepared by professionals in those fields, and without our tinkering with those reports we sent them to New York headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: In the reports that you received from the ground, did you have any reason to believe that any of those reports you were receiving were inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no reason to believe that they were inaccurate. Of course, you had to always make allowance for honest human errors, misunderstandings, and, you know, absolute objectivity may be sometimes very hard to attain. But as a matter of -- falsely based ourselves on the impartiality and objectivity of our colleagues, all of whom are working for the United Nations or for very similar organisations, like ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that answer, Mr. Akashi. I want to move through a few documents as quickly as possible. I am going to do my upmost to try to complete in the next 15 minutes so that hopefully you don't have to come back tomorrow, pending any questions from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to co-operate also.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I have to doubt that you will, Mr. Akashi. If we can go to D1213, which is tab 8 of the Prosecution binder.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for it to come here on the screen for everyone to follow. But if you can go to page 3 after having looked at the cover sheet and confirm that it is one of the cables that you sent. If you go to the third page, the last paragraph it says: "On more general topic, Mr. Bildt noted that in a meeting with Dr. Granic over the weekend, the latter had said that he believed 99 per cent of the population in the Krajina would leave Croatia (our figure was slightly lower). Granic had also indicated that the Croatian military plan had been designed to facilitate their departure - a form of ethnic cleansing by other means, in Mr. Bildt's opinion." Mr. Akashi, do you remember having this discussion with Mr. Bildt after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall this particular discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can then move to the next tab in the Prosecution binder, which is tab 9, which is 65 ter 4129.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I will just wait for it to come up here so everyone can follow. It seem that the electronic version is slower than the physical. There we go. We have it now. It's another cable from you on the 23rd of August. In paragraph three, there is reference there: "Also noteworthy, however, is that a Croatian civil defence officially present at the site" -- And I'm sorry but by way of background, this discusses graves in the Knin cemetery. Said that most of the deceased were civilians from Knin who had been killed during the Croatian shelling of the city on 4 and 5 August. And then for the last line of the page: "Pending further evidence, there is no basis to conclude at this point that those," turn the page over, "buried in the Knin cemetery died as a result of executions rather than shelling of civilian areas of Knin." Mr. Akashi, do you know whether such a determination was made later regarding the cause of death of the individuals in the Knin cemetery?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection with regard to this particular event.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If I can tendered 65 ter 4129 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, my recollection is this is already in evidence. So if it can be MFI'd and we can check on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It may be duplicate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we have a 65 ter number, I take it that Mr. Registrar can verify within just a couple of seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I just find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It is P2629 and it is not me who found it by our Case Manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is, therefore, no reason not to move on. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That would be the new number for this exhibit; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This 65 ter number is not known under any exhibit number and, therefore, number then to be assigned would be 2629; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. That will be Exhibit P2629.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections Mr. Misetic? Then P2629 is, after some confusion, admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we can go to tab 20 of the Prosecution binder this time and it is 65 ter 7402. It's a weekly situation report from yourself to Mr. Annan dated 29 August. As we will see when it comes on the screen it covers the period 22 to 28 August. And if we go to the next page, page 2 of this document, in the first paragraph, there's a sentence that starts: "Tudjman dismissed the reports of burning houses and looting as the acts of individuals which were condemned by the government. He reiterated his appeal that the houses of Serbs should not be destroyed - Croatian displaced people would have to be accommodated in the abandoned houses."

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you remember this statement from President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot -- I beg your pardon, but I cannot locate that passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Sure. It is in the first full paragraph under, "Croatia." It is the sixth or seventh line, which starts, "Tudjman dismissed reports ..." I won't read again. Just read those two sentences for yourself --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: -- and let me know if you remember this statement.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. I do not specifically remember these words, but it seems to convey the general sense of our discussions with President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If I can tender 65 ter 7402 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2630.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can then move to a document we looked at earlier today, D1665, that is at tab 43 in the Defence binder, which is the further report prepared by the Secretary-General to the Security Council. And I would like to go to paragraph 5, which was briefly mentioned --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: -- but I want to ask you about a specific passage: "Secondly, in the course of the Croatian Army's recapture of Sectors North and South, more than 90 per cent of the ... Serb inhabitants fled from those areas. Though it was hoped that some of the Serb refugee would return to their homes, the continued reports of human rights abuses and of the looting and burning of houses have created a climate which is not conducive to such a development. Indeed, many Serbs from among those who initially chose to remain are now departing or seeking to depart owing to the hostile environment in which they are at present obliged to live." Now, Mr. Akashi, do you -- do you remember that general situation in the Krajina after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And is that consistent with your recollection of that general situation?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, as reflected in the paragraph you drew our attention to, just -- just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. I just have a few more questions with respect to General Cermak. In your -- in your cables and we have looked at a number of them so far today, some we have not seen but are in evidence. And in those cables and in the interests of time I won't go through each of them with you, you described General Cermak sometimes as the Croatian Army commander for the Knin region; sometimes as the HV commander for the region; sometimes as the Croatian Army commander in the area; some other times as the military official in charge of the region. Now I understand that those may not have always been your words, but can you tell us what was your understanding of General Cermak's role in Knin, after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Sure. I have described to you the different ways in which -- I have read to you the different ways in which General Cermak is described in your cables as Croatian Army commander for the region, for the area, military official in charge of the region and I was asking you if you have -- what is your memory of the understanding of what General Cermak's role was or position was in Knin, after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After, did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Well, when he arrived in Knin after Operation Storm or -- right after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have referred to various different ways of the military commander of the Croatian Army in the Knin area described in our cables, and so we did not necessarily link all these actions to a single person or a military leader or commander. We were talking about specific actions, specific instances of use of force or violence, which was a manifestation of organised use of force; and so we did not necessarily personalise and link these to the act or actions of one individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Akashi, just one last question. When you met General Cermak on 7th of August, did you consider him to be a military person?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But I do not necessarily have fixed ideas about a military person, as against a civilian person. Some military person may be more civilian, more humanitarian than usual civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, thank you very much for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedaraly. Could I inquire with the parties how much time needed for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Nothing, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: None, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, I would have a few questions for you but I wonder whether you would be available for another, perhaps, ten minutes so usually we stop --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, I am. I'm at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it might save you coming back tomorrow, Mr. Akashi. I have the following question for you. Could we have D28 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, you will remember that this is the agreement, if I could briefly refer to it as the Akashi-Sarinic agreement. In paragraph 3 of this agreement, reference is made to encouragement "of all those previous inhabitants of the Republic of Croatia who so wish to remain peacefully in the areas ..." "All those previous inhabitants," how did you understand this? Would that refer, in your recollection, to those who had been living in the RSK area, which was --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- which particular paragraph of the agreement are you referring?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, second line.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The previous inhabitants, did you consider them to be those who lived in the RSK before Operation Storm; or would you consider them to be those who had lived in the Krajina area before 1991? How did you understand and how did you intend to agree on the wording "previous inhabitants of the Republic of Croatia"?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just, in my own mind, I did not have a particular, specific time or timing in which they have lived in the Krajinas. English is not my native tongue, nor is it Mr. Sarinic's native tongue, I take it, although his English was much better than mine. So, at least in my mind, it has meant those who have lived, those Serbs who have lived in the Krajinas, up to that time, can remain doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just ... well, of course, I asked you, because under those circumstances, you could have referred to the Serb inhabitants of the Krajina. I am especially interested to know what was specifically meant by the word "previous." Previous referring to earlier time, and, of course, I'm interested to know whether it was recent past or those who had been inhabitants in a period which was further away in history; that is before 1991.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have a very sharp legal mind, which I don't, and I have -- I -- I thought it meant those who have lived there, up to that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. I don't know whether the parties disagree with one of your recent observations, but that is not to be discussed at this moment. Then I have one other question to you in ... yes, I would like to take you, again in D28, to paragraph 5. Paragraph 5 deals with the freedom of movement: "Immediately in all areas," as it reads "except where, in the opinion of the local UNCRO military commanders after consulting Croatian Army commanders, the security situation does not permit for such surveillance." Now, ample time has been spent on your meeting with, among others, General Cermak on the basis of the notes of Mr. Almstrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Bambury, My Lord. Bambury.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he was, as a matter of fact, I was referring to an observation by Mr. Almstrom, but you're right in correcting me. Could we have that -- I have not written down the exhibit number, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1667. Could we have that and could we move to the page with last four ERN digits, 6920. We read on this page, that, as of tomorrow, that the UN would -- agencies would have freedom of movement in and around Knin; and the day after, larger areas, depending on security. Now, did you consider a position in which the Croatian authorities said that they would allow, depending on security, a wider freedom of movement consistent with paragraph 5 of the agreement where it was left to the UNCRO command, after consultation with the Croatian military leadership, to determine whether or not security would allow freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I'm not a lawyer with a sharp legal mind, but I thought, at that time, that our discussions in Knin were in accordance with the agreement we -- I had reached with Mr. Sarinic. If my very scarce legal training at the graduate school serves me, there's a difference between two phrases: One, "in consultation with"; and the other is "after consultation with." The difference being that "in consult with" means you had to be in continuous consultation with that person; where "after consultation" means that you consult with somebody but your subsequent action may not necessarily be in conformity with your previous talks. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether you are correct or not, you have explained your position in this respect. Of course, the language in paragraph 5 is somewhere in between. It uses the words "after." But it also said says "after consulting" and not "after having consulted." Let's leave it to that. You have given your answer. I have no further questions for you, Mr. Akashi. Have the questions by the Bench triggered any need to put further questions to Mr. Akashi? Mr. Akashi --- I apologise for first addressing our interpreters, transcriber, and those who are assisting in this courtroom because I went - and I have a bad reputation in this respect - I went 17 minutes beyond the time that was available to us. At the same time, it saves us and saves you from having to come back tomorrow so, therefore, my apologies to interpreters, transcribers. Mr. Akashi, I would like to thank you very much for reserving time in your busy schedule for coming to testify, and you've answered the questions put to you by the Bench and by the parties. The Bench is - and I take it the parties - are grateful for that. You are excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, My Honour. I hope my answers did not seem to be excessively evasive but this was due to a lot of time which has transpired between today and when events actually took place, and you understand extremely complex difficult circumstances in which United Nations had to operate with its very rather unclear mandate and with its very limited resources. But there should be no question as to one point, that it was with our utmost commitment to the cause of peace, to the cause of humanity, that we did our very best, which is not good enough in the opinion of some. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Akashi. I usually wish those who have testified a safe trip home again. In view of your schedule, I don't know whether you are going home or for somewhere else, but wherever you go, arrive safely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You are most gracious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we can conclude the videolink with Tokyo. For you, Mr. Registrar, in Tokyo, we don't need the technical facilities any longer because -- well, I don't have to explain that to you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn for the day. The Chamber had in mind to find time for a housekeeping session before the start of the Cermak case. Therefore, I think it is important to establish, Mr. Misetic, that this was the last witness you wanted to call in the presentation of the Gotovina Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it might be good that we reserve some time to go through pending issues, lists, MFI's et cetera. In order to be properly prepared, the Chamber would prefer to do that on Friday. I am aware that it would keep you here for the Thursday, but experience has taught us that if we are not really prepared for that, it creates more confusion than it resolves; and, therefore, I would like to prepare that tomorrow and then have a housekeeping session Friday morning. Would that meet any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: There are no objections on our part. I don't know if Mr. Monkhouse needs to be involved or if someone else can assist from the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is exactly -- I started only by saying that is what we had on our mind. Since we have to expect that Mr. Monkhouse has not returned by Friday morning, at least there is an considerable risk that he has not, it might be that we cannot deal with everything because an experienced Registrar is of greatest assistance, and that is especially also one of the issues I'd like to include in the Chamber's preparations of tomorrow. So whether we can deal with everything or if we would conclude that it isn't worthwhile even to give it a try on Friday, then the Chamber would, of course, inform the parties, and then we would have to move to early next week. So, therefore, as matters stand now, we will adjourn until Friday, the 18th of September, Courtroom I, for a housekeeping session; and if that would change, the Chamber will immediately inform the parties, in which case we would resume only after the UN holiday, which is on the 21st of September, Monday, and we would then be in Courtroom III at 9.00 on the 22nd of September. Any questions in relation to this? If not, we stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 18th day of September, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
